chapter.name: A Journey through States of Water
chapter.blurb: Water disappears from open surfaces by evaporation (turning into invisible water vapour), and water vapour turns back into liquid droplets by condensation on a cold surface. Water's three states -- solid, liquid, gas -- differ in shape, flow and spread; heating melts a solid and cooling freezes a liquid. Evaporation speed depends on surface area, temperature, wind and humidity, and evaporation has a cooling effect that also drives the water cycle: evaporation, condensation into clouds, and rain.

scope_in.item: Evaporation: the conversion of water into its vapour state; water vapour is normally invisible, though droplets in steam can make it visible; everyday examples include drying clothes, a mopped floor drying, and sweat drying
Investigating whether disappearing water seeps away or evaporates, using the steel-plate activity where water disappears without seeping through

Condensation: the conversion of water vapour into its liquid state, occurring when water vapour touches a cold surface, e.g. droplets on a cold glass tumbler, dew on plants, or drops on the underside of a lid over boiling water

Using a marked water level and the total mass of a setup (via a weighing balance) to distinguish condensation of water vapour from the air from seepage out of a container; humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air

Three states of water -- solid (ice), liquid (water), gas (water vapour) -- and their properties: ice keeps its shape and does not flow or spread; water has no fixed shape, flows, spreads, and keeps a constant volume; water vapour has no fixed shape and spreads to fill all available space; other substances (wax, oil, ghee) also show these three states
Melting (solid to liquid, by supplying heat) and freezing (liquid to solid, by removing heat), with examples beyond water: candle wax and coconut oil

Conditions affecting the rate of evaporation: a larger exposed surface area speeds it up; higher temperature/sunlight speeds it up; more air movement (wind) speeds it up; higher humidity slows it down (e.g. clothes dry more slowly on a rainy, humid day)

Evaporation has a cooling effect (e.g. an earthen pot/surahi keeps water cool as it seeps and evaporates, sanitiser feels cool on the hands, sweat cools the body, especially when helped by a fan or wind)

How clouds form and give rain: rising air cools, water vapour condenses into droplets generally around dust particles, forming clouds; droplets join into bigger, heavier drops that fall as rain (also hail or snow under special conditions); water vapour is lighter than air, so it rises
The water cycle: the continuous circulation of water between the Earth's surface and the atmosphere through evaporation and condensation

concepts.name: Evaporation: water changing into vapour
concepts.description: Water left exposed gradually converts into invisible water vapour, a process called evaporation, distinct from water seeping away.
concepts.idea: When water is left exposed, it gradually disappears by converting into an invisible gaseous form called water vapour; this process is called evaporation.
concepts.rule: Water does not usually disappear by seeping away, as shown by the steel-plate activity where it does not pass through to the other side; instead it evaporates into the air as water vapour, which is normally invisible.
concepts.example: Water puddles on a playground disappear over the day due to evaporation; drying of wet clothes, a mopped floor, and sweat on the body are all everyday examples.

concepts.name: Condensation: water vapour changing into liquid
concepts.description: Water vapour touching a cold surface turns into liquid droplets, a process called condensation, distinguishable from a leak by checking the water level and total mass.
concepts.idea: When water vapour present in the air touches a cold surface, it changes back into tiny liquid water droplets; this process is called condensation.
concepts.rule: Condensation can be told apart from seepage by checking whether the original water level actually decreases -- if the water level inside a container stays the same while droplets form outside, and the total mass increases, the droplets came from condensation, not seepage.
concepts.example: Water droplets form on the outside of a glass tumbler of ice-cold water because water vapour in the air condenses on the cold surface; the mass of the tumbler setup increases over time, confirming this.

concepts.name: Three states of water: solid, liquid and gas
concepts.description: Water exists as solid ice, liquid water and gaseous water vapour, each with distinct shape, flow and spreading behaviour.
concepts.idea: Water exists in three states in daily life -- solid (ice), liquid (water) and gas (water vapour) -- and each state behaves differently in shape, flowing and spreading.
concepts.rule: Ice keeps its own shape, does not flow and does not spread; water has no fixed shape but keeps a constant volume, flows and can spread; water vapour has no fixed shape and spreads out to fill all available space.
concepts.example: Ice keeps its cube shape when moved to a new container, water poured into a differently shaped container takes on that shape while its amount stays the same, and water vapour in the air spreads invisibly throughout a room.

concepts.name: Changing states of water: melting and freezing
concepts.description: Supplying heat melts a solid into a liquid; removing heat freezes a liquid into a solid, a behaviour shown by water and other substances alike.
concepts.idea: Supplying heat converts a solid to a liquid (and a liquid further to a gas); removing heat converts a gas to a liquid and a liquid to a solid.
concepts.rule: The conversion of a solid into its liquid state is called melting; the conversion of a liquid into its solid state is called freezing. Other substances besides water, such as candle wax and coconut oil, also show these changes.
concepts.example: Ice at room temperature melts into water by gaining heat; water in a freezer freezes into ice by losing heat; melted candle wax cools and freezes back into solid wax.

questions.q: Explain why melting and freezing are described as opposite processes to each other.
questions.a: Melting converts a solid into a liquid by supplying heat, while freezing converts a liquid into a solid by removing heat; since one process adds heat to cause a solid-to-liquid change and the other removes heat to cause the reverse liquid-to-solid change, they are opposite processes of each other.

questions.q: A friend says, 'Only water can melt and freeze; other substances just stay the way they are.' Do you agree with this statement? Justify your answer using examples from the chapter.
questions.a: No, I disagree. questions.q: Invent a short quiz game, describing its rules, that tests classmates on whether a described change is melting or freezing, using five everyday examples of your choice.

s: Describes a workable game format/rules
Provides at least five relevant, varied everyday examples
Correctly identifies melt/freeze for the examples given

concepts.name: Conditions that affect the rate of evaporation
concepts.description: Evaporation speeds up with a larger exposed area, higher temperature and more wind, and slows down with higher humidity.
concepts.idea: How fast water evaporates depends on several conditions: the exposed surface area, the temperature, the movement of air, and the humidity.
concepts.rule: Evaporation is faster with a larger exposed surface area, higher temperature and more wind; it is slower when humidity is higher, since the air already holds a lot of water vapour.
concepts.example: Water spread on a plate evaporates faster than the same amount in a bottle cap, because of the larger area; clothes dry faster on a hot, windy day than on a cool, rainy, humid day.

questions.q: Design a fair investigation, different from the ones in the book, to test how humidity affects the speed of evaporation, keeping the surface area, temperature and wind conditions the same in both setups.
questions.a: Sample: Place two identical open dishes of the same amount of water in two rooms of the same temperature with no wind or fans -- one room with a humidifier or damp cloths to raise humidity, and one room kept at normal humidity. questions.q: Explain why a scientist testing the effect of wind on evaporation rate must keep the exposed surface area and temperature the same in both setups being compared.

questions.q: A friend claims, 'Wind is the only thing that affects how fast water evaporates; temperature, surface area and humidity don't matter.' Evaluate this claim using ideas from the chapter.
questions.a: This claim is not correct. Evaporation speed is affected by several conditions together: a larger exposed surface area speeds up evaporation, higher temperature speeds it up, wind speeds it up by carrying away nearby water vapour, and higher humidity slows it down since the air already holds a lot of water vapour; wind is only one of several factors, not the only one.
s: States the claim is incorrect
Names at least two other correct factors besides wind
Explains at least one factor's effect correctly

questions.q: Design a short evaporation-rate checklist or rating scale, described in words, that someone could use to quickly predict whether laundry will dry fast or slow on a given day.
questions.a: Sample checklist: Rate each condition as favourable (+1) or unfavourable (0) for fast drying: (1) Is it sunny/hot? (2) Is it windy? (3) Is the laundry spread out with a large exposed area? (4) Is the air dry (low humidity)? Add up the points from 0 to 4; a higher score predicts faster drying, and a lower score predicts slower drying.
s: Includes surface area as a checklist factor
Includes temperature/sunlight and wind as checklist factors
Includes humidity as a checklist factor, and gives a sensible way to combine/score them

concepts.name: Evaporation's cooling effect and the water cycle
concepts.description: Evaporation cools its surroundings, and the same evaporation-condensation cycle drives the water cycle, moving water between the Earth's surface and clouds as rain.
concepts.idea: Evaporation has a cooling effect, since converting a liquid into vapour uses up heat from its surroundings; the same evaporation-condensation cycle drives the water cycle.
concepts.rule: An earthen pot keeps water cool because water seeping through its porous surface evaporates and cools the water inside; the water cycle is the continuous circulation of water between the Earth's surface and the atmosphere through evaporation and condensation.
concepts.example: Sweat evaporating from the skin cools the body; high in the atmosphere, air cools until its water vapour condenses into droplets around tiny dust particles, forming clouds, and heavy droplets eventually fall as rain.

questions.q: Explain how evaporation and condensation, which seem like opposite processes, both play essential roles in the same water cycle.
questions.a: Evaporation converts liquid water from the Earth's surface into water vapour that rises into the atmosphere, while condensation later converts that rising water vapour back into liquid droplets that form clouds and eventually fall as rain; both processes are needed together to complete the full cycle of water moving from the surface to the atmosphere and back again.
s: Correctly describes evaporation's role (surface water to vapour, rising)
Correctly describes condensation's role (vapour to droplets/clouds, falling as rain) and links both as necessary for the cycle

questions.q: A friend says, 'The water cycle is basically just rain falling from the sky; evaporation and condensation are not really that important.' Do you agree? Justify your answer.
questions.a: No, I disagree. Rain is only the final visible step of the water cycle; without evaporation first lifting water from oceans, lakes and other surfaces into the atmosphere as invisible water vapour, and without condensation later turning that vapour into droplets that form clouds, there would be no water high in the atmosphere to fall as rain in the first place -- all three processes are essential and connected.
s: States disagreement with the claim
Explains evaporation's essential role in supplying water vapour to the atmosphere
Explains condensation's essential role in forming the clouds that produce rain

questions.q: Invent a short role-play script, describing the characters and their lines, that a group of students could perform to act out the journey of a water molecule through the water cycle, from the ocean to a cloud and back as rain.
questions.a: Sample: Character 'Ocean Water' begins lying down centre stage. As 'Sun' character waves warm hands over it, 'Ocean Water' stands up and floats away as 'Water Vapour,' rising slowly. As it reaches 'Cold Sky' character, it huddles together with other 'Water Vapour' actors around a 'Dust Particle' character to become 'Cloud Droplets.' When enough droplets have gathered, they fall together as 'Raindrops,' running back to rejoin 'Ocean Water' at the start.
s: Correctly includes evaporation (water rising due to heat)
Correctly includes condensation around dust particles forming a cloud
Correctly includes rain falling and returning the water to the surface, completing the cycle
